newsitem.title: USA: Republicans hope budget passes without controversy.
newsitem.headline: Republicans hope budget passes without controversy.

text.p: Senate Republicans said on Tuesday they were attempting to reach agreement with Democrats to give final approval this week to the fiscal 1998 budget.

But Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle told reporters they wanted to offer amendments when the measure comes before the Senate. Both the House and Senate approved the budget last month by wide bipartisan margins, but this final version must pass each chamber again.
Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, said he wanted it to clear the Senate without amendments to avoid sending it back to the House for a vote.
Democrats hope to add a non-binding resolution urging the Senate to act quickly on disaster aid for the flood-ravaged northern Midwest and other states, a Democratic source said.

Under Senate rules, Democrats cannot hold up passage of the budget to try to force action on the disaster relief legislation. It provides $5.5 billion in disaster aid and $1.9 billion to pay for already incurred costs of U.S. military operations in Bosnia and the Gulf.
However, Daschle told reporters Democrats were intent upon forcing action on the disaster relief legislation.

"We're contemplating the use of any available vehicle to make our case as loudly and clearly as we can, until we get that resolved, we're not going to be sympathetic to moving any legislation along," the South Dakota Democrat said.
The disaster relief legislation has become entangled in a dispute over Republican efforts to use it to avert another government shutdown.

The budget is a non-binding blueprint for spending and taxes. Worked out over several months with the White House and both parties in Congress, it calls for a net $85 billion in tax cuts over the next five years, $115 billion in Medicare cuts over five years and a slower rate of growth for other government programs.
Congress will spend the rest of this session working out some 15 separate bills needed to enact the budget into law.

The first two of these, the tax bill and the Medicare legislation, are to be worked out in committees starting this month. The regular 13 appropriations bills covering spending for fiscal 1998 must be approved by Oct 1 or the government risks another partial shutdown.
